about: Evidence Builder (docs/appsych-spec.md sections 3.2 and 6; builder T1). Each context is one evidence-based question with three invented sources; the model (psychology/assets/tools/math/evidence-builder.js) draws the sources' numbers from ApPsychStats, scores a built answer on the 7-point rubric and builds the drills. Every source is invented for practice (decision 4) and says so on the page.
intro:
The evidence-based question (EBQ) gives you three sources and asks for a claim, two pieces of evidence from two different sources, and reasoning that links each one to the claim with a psychology concept. It is worth 7 points and, on the 2025 exam, students scored lower on it than on the article analysis question.

Build an answer from the pieces: pick a claim, pick each piece of evidence (and whether you cite it), pick the concept that explains it. The score updates as you build, and every lost point names the slip.
howItWorks:
The sources are invented for practice, written in the layout the exam uses, and their numbers are computed with the course's statistics code each time you open a question, so the graphs and the results always agree.

The score follows the 2025 and 2026 scoring guidelines, in our own words: A (1 point) a defensible claim, not a topic, a question or an oversimplified statement; B(i) and C(i) (1 point each) a specific result, cited, that supports the claim, from two different sources; B(ii) and C(ii) (2 points each) one point for linking the evidence to the claim and the second for a psychology concept that explains it. A research or statistics word, or the question's own topic, never counts as the concept, and C(ii) needs a different concept from B(ii). If the claim misses, A scores 0 but B and C can still score: the scoring guidelines let your evidence and reasoning set up the claim you meant.

The builder checks your choices exactly; the box for writing your own reasoning only gives hints (a citation, a concept, a restricted term) and never a score.

contexts.title: Other people and stress
contexts.question: Does support from other people reduce stress?

claims.text: Support from other people can reduce how much stress a person feels.
claims.generic: Friends are good for people, so they make life better.

claims.text: Having a friend nearby can calm the body's response to a stressful moment.
claims.generic: Friends are nice to have around when things are hard.

claims.why: This names the topic but takes no position. A claim is a statement the sources can support.
A question is not a claim. Answer it: say what the sources show.

claims.text: Anyone with friends never feels stressed.
claims.why: Oversimplified: no source shows that stress disappears, and none studied everyone. Make a claim the sources can defend.

claims.text: Source 3 assigned nursing students to study groups.
claims.why: This summarizes a source's method. A claim answers the question in your own words.

sources.title: A speech, alone or with a friend
sources.intro: A friend's presence may change how strongly the body reacts to a stressor.
sources.participants: Forty-eight adults (ages 20 to 35) in Chicago, recruited online; each brought a close friend.
sources.method: Participants were randomly assigned to give a five-minute speech to two strangers either alone or with their friend sitting in the room. Heart rate was measured with a chest monitor before and during the speech.
sources.detail: Forty-eight adults in Chicago each brought a close friend to the study.
sources.vague: having a friend there made a difference.
sources.res: Heart rate rose by a mean of {m0} beats per minute for participants who spoke alone and {m1} for those whose friend was present.
sources.ev: participants who gave a speech with a friend present had a smaller rise in heart rate ({m1} beats per minute) than participants who were alone ({m0})
sources.axis: Mean rise in heart rate (beats per minute)

sources.title: Friends on campus and daily stress
sources.intro: Starting college brings many small daily stressors.
sources.participants: Sixty first-year students (ages 18 and 19) at one university in Georgia.
sources.method: In October, students reported how many close friends they had on campus and rated their stress each evening for two weeks from 1 (none) to 10 (extreme); the ratings were averaged.
sources.detail: Sixty first-year students in Georgia rated their stress every evening for two weeks.
sources.res: The correlation between the number of close friends on campus and the average daily stress rating was r = {r}.
sources.ev: first-year students with more close friends on campus tended to rate their daily stress lower (r = {r})

sources.title: Study groups in exam week
sources.intro: Exam week is a common stressor for students in demanding programs.
sources.participants: Seventy nursing students (ages 19 to 24) at two colleges in Arizona.
sources.method: Students were randomly assigned to meet with a peer study group twice during exam week or to study alone. On the last day of exams, each rated their stress for the week from 1 (none) to 10 (extreme).
sources.detail: Seventy nursing students at two Arizona colleges took part during exam week.
sources.vague: the study groups changed how the week went.
sources.res: Students who studied alone gave a mean stress rating of {m0}, and students in study groups gave a mean rating of {m1}.
sources.ev: nursing students who met with a study group rated their exam-week stress lower ({m1}) than students who studied alone ({m0})

concepts.name: the sympathetic nervous system
concepts.def: The sympathetic nervous system is the part of the autonomic nervous system that arouses the body.

links.0: a speech arouses the sympathetic nervous system and speeds the heart, and a smaller rise with a friend present means less arousal, so support reduced the body's stress response.

concepts.off: It describes the body's arousal, and this source measured ratings or friendships, not the body.

concepts.name: the fight-flight-freeze response
concepts.def: The fight-flight-freeze response is the body's automatic reaction to a threat.

links.0: the speech set off a fight-flight-freeze response, and its heart-rate surge was smaller with a friend present, so support softened the stress response.

concepts.off: It is the body's reaction to a threat, and this source did not measure the body.

concepts.name: emotion-focused coping
concepts.def: Emotion-focused coping means managing the feelings a stressor causes.

links.1: friends give students someone to share their feelings with, a form of emotion-focused coping, so students with more friends feel less daily stress.
links.2: a study group lets students talk through their worries together, a form of emotion-focused coping, so they felt less stressed.

concepts.off: Coping is about how a person handles a stressor over time; this source measured one moment in the body.

concepts.name: problem-focused coping
concepts.def: Problem-focused coping means acting on the stressor itself.

links.2: the study group worked on the stressor itself, preparing for the exams, which is problem-focused coping, so the students felt less stressed.
links.1: close friends can help a student solve everyday problems directly, problem-focused coping, which fits the lower daily stress of students with more friends.

concepts.off: Problem-focused coping acts on the stressor, and nobody acted on the speech in this source.

concepts.name: the tend-and-befriend response
concepts.def: The tend-and-befriend response is reaching out to others under stress.
concepts.off: It describes people choosing to seek out others under stress, and no source let participants choose: the friend or the group was assigned, or friendships were only counted.

contexts.title: Sleep loss and thinking
contexts.question: Does losing sleep harm how well people think and remember?

claims.text: Losing sleep harms people's thinking, including memory and attention.
claims.generic: Sleep is important, so everyone should get more of it.

claims.text: Losing sleep makes it harder to hold on to and use information.
claims.generic: Tired people are not at their best.

claims.why: This names the topic but takes no position. A claim is a statement the sources can support.

claims.text: How much sleep do people need?
claims.why: A question is not a claim, and this one is not what the prompt asks.

claims.text: One night without sleep ruins a person's memory for good.
claims.why: Oversimplified: the sources tested days, not a lifetime. Make a claim the sources can defend.

claims.text: Source 2 kept adults awake for 24 hours.
claims.why: This summarizes a source's method. A claim answers the question in your own words.

sources.title: Sleep after learning
sources.intro: Sleep after learning may help new memories last.
sources.participants: Fifty-two university students (ages 18 to 23) in Oregon.
sources.method: Students learned 30 word pairs at 9 p.m. They were randomly assigned to sleep in the lab or to stay awake until 5 a.m. Recall was tested two days later, after everyone had slept normally the night between.
sources.detail: Fifty-two university students in Oregon learned 30 word pairs at 9 p.m.
sources.res: Students who slept after learning recalled a mean of {m0} word pairs, and students kept awake recalled a mean of {m1}.
sources.ev: students who slept after learning recalled more word pairs two days later ({m0}) than students kept awake that night ({m1})

sources.title: A day without sleep
sources.intro: Many jobs require people to stay alert after a long time awake.
sources.participants: Forty adults (ages 25 to 45) in Boston who said they usually sleep 7 to 9 hours.
sources.method: Adults were randomly assigned to a full night of sleep or to stay awake for 24 hours in the lab. Then each did a 10-minute task: press a button whenever a light appears. A lapse was a response slower than half a second.
sources.detail: Forty adults in Boston who usually sleep 7 to 9 hours took part.
sources.vague: the adults did worse on a task.
sources.res: Adults kept awake for 24 hours had a mean of {m0} lapses, and adults who slept had a mean of {m1}.
sources.ev: adults kept awake for 24 hours had more attention lapses on a 10-minute task ({m0}) than adults who had slept ({m1})

sources.title: School-night sleep and working memory
sources.intro: Many teenagers sleep less than recommended on school nights.
sources.participants: Seventy high school students (ages 14 to 18) in Wisconsin.
sources.method: Students wore sleep trackers for two weeks; the researchers averaged their sleep on school nights. Then each took a working-memory test: repeating longer and longer strings of digits backward (score 0 to 12).
sources.detail: Seventy Wisconsin high school students wore sleep trackers for two weeks.
sources.vague: sleep was linked to the test.
sources.res: The correlation between average school-night sleep and working-memory score was r = {r}.
sources.ev: high school students who slept more on school nights tended to score higher on a working-memory test (r = {r})

concepts.name: consolidation theory
concepts.def: Consolidation theory says that sleep helps store memories.

links.0: by consolidation theory, sleep strengthens new memories, so students who slept after learning held on to more word pairs than those kept awake.

concepts.off: Consolidation is about storing new memories after learning, and this source did not test new learning.

concepts.name: memory consolidation
concepts.def: Memory consolidation is the process that makes a new memory stable.

links.0: staying awake disrupted memory consolidation, so the word pairs were less stable and fewer were recalled two days later.

concepts.off: This source did not test whether new memories were stored.

concepts.name: restoration theory
concepts.def: Restoration theory says sleep restores the body and brain.

links.1: by restoration theory, sleep restores the brain; without it, adults' attention lapsed more often, so losing sleep harms thinking.
links.2: by restoration theory, sleep restores the brain each night, which fits teenagers with more sleep scoring higher on a working-memory test.

concepts.off: Restoration is about recovery from being awake, and this source tested storing new information.

concepts.name: attention
concepts.def: Attention is focusing awareness on part of what is around you.

links.1: lapses are failures of attention, so more lapses after 24 hours awake show that sleep loss harms the ability to focus.

concepts.off: This source measured recall or a memory span, not focus over time.

concepts.name: working memory
concepts.def: Working memory holds and works on information for a short time.

links.2: repeating digits backward uses working memory, and teenagers who slept more held and used more digits, so sleep loss fits weaker working memory.

concepts.off: This source did not test holding and working on information in the moment.

contexts.title: Rewards and motivation
contexts.question: Do rewards increase people's motivation to do a task?

claims.text: Whether a reward raises or lowers motivation depends on whether people already enjoy the task.
claims.generic: Rewards are good sometimes and bad other times.

claims.text: Rewards can lower people's motivation to do something they already enjoy.
claims.generic: People should not be paid for things they like.

claims.text: Rewards and how they affect people.
claims.why: This names the topic but takes no position. A claim is a statement the sources can support.

claims.text: Should schools pay students for good grades?
claims.why: A question is not a claim, and this one goes beyond the prompt.
Oversimplified, and Source 1 contradicts it. Make a claim all your evidence can defend.

claims.text: Source 2 paid adults to enter data.
claims.why: This summarizes a source's method. A claim answers the question in your own words.

sources.title: Drawing for a reward
sources.intro: Children who already enjoy an activity may react differently when they are rewarded for it.
sources.participants: Fifty-six preschool children (ages 4 and 5) in Vermont whose teachers said they liked drawing.
sources.method: Children were randomly assigned to draw for six minutes after being promised a certificate (the reward group) or with no reward mentioned. Two weeks later, observers timed how long each child chose to draw during a free-play hour.
sources.detail: Fifty-six preschool children in Vermont who liked drawing took part.
sources.vague: the reward changed the children's drawing.
sources.res: During free play, children who had expected no reward drew for a mean of {m0} minutes, and children who had expected a reward drew for {m1} minutes.
sources.ev: children who had been promised a reward for drawing later chose to draw less in free play ({m1} minutes) than children promised nothing ({m0} minutes)
sources.axis: Mean minutes drawing in free play

sources.title: Pay for a dull task
sources.intro: Some work is repetitive and few people would do it for fun.
sources.participants: Sixty adults (ages 21 to 60) hired online in the United States for a one-hour task.
sources.method: Adults were randomly assigned to earn a flat fee or a flat fee plus 5 cents for every form they completed. For one hour they copied information from scanned forms into a spreadsheet.
sources.detail: Sixty adults were hired online for a one-hour data-entry task.
sources.vague: pay changed how the adults worked.
sources.res: Adults paid per form completed a mean of {m0} forms, and adults paid a flat fee completed a mean of {m1}.
sources.ev: adults paid for every form they completed finished more forms in an hour ({m0}) than adults paid a flat fee ({m1})
sources.axis: Mean forms completed in one hour

sources.title: Why students study
sources.intro: College students study for many reasons, from interest in the subject to grades and future pay.
sources.participants: One hundred twenty college students (ages 18 to 25) at a university in Texas.
sources.method: Students rated how much they study for outside rewards such as grades or pay (1 to 7) and how much they enjoy their major (1 to 7).
sources.detail: One hundred twenty college students in Texas filled out two questionnaires.
sources.res: The correlation between studying for outside rewards and enjoying the major was r = {r}.
sources.ev: college students who said they study mainly for outside rewards tended to enjoy their major less (r = {r})

concepts.name: the overjustification effect
concepts.def: The overjustification effect is when a reward lowers interest in something a person already enjoyed.

links.0: promising a reward for drawing, which the children already enjoyed, produced the overjustification effect: they drew less once the reward was gone, so a reward lowered their motivation.

concepts.off: It applies to rewarding a task people already enjoy, and this task was not one they enjoyed.

concepts.name: intrinsic motivation
concepts.def: Intrinsic motivation is the desire to do something for its own sake.

links.0: the children drew for fun, which is intrinsic motivation; the reward undercut it, so they chose to draw less later.
links.2: students who study mainly for rewards have less intrinsic motivation, which fits their enjoying their major less.

concepts.off: Copying forms is not done for its own sake, so intrinsic motivation does not explain this result.

concepts.name: extrinsic motivation
concepts.def: Extrinsic motivation is the desire to do something for a reward.

links.1: pay for each form is extrinsic motivation, and on a dull task it raised effort, so rewards increased motivation when the task was not enjoyed.

concepts.off: This result shows enjoyment falling, which extrinsic motivation alone does not explain.

concepts.name: incentive theory
concepts.def: Incentive theory says that people are pulled toward behaviors by rewards.

links.1: by incentive theory, the 5 cents per form pulled adults toward completing more forms, so a reward increased motivation for a dull task.

concepts.off: Here the reward did not pull behavior up.

concepts.name: positive reinforcement
concepts.def: Positive reinforcement is adding something pleasant after a behavior so it happens more often.

links.1: each completed form was followed by pay, positive reinforcement, so completing forms happened more often.

concepts.off: Here a reward was followed by less of the behavior, the opposite of reinforcement.

concepts.name: self-determination theory
concepts.def: Self-determination theory says people need autonomy, competence and relatedness.

links.2: by self-determination theory, studying for outside rewards leaves students feeling less in control (autonomy), which fits their enjoying their major less.

concepts.off: This source did not measure the needs the theory names.
